BLUE HAS A FOOTHOLD IN THE EAST. TRY TO DESTROY IT AS QUICKLY 
AS POSSIBLE.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.0.31.0.messa: You encounter someone who looks like a young man. He has both a beard and breasts! Seeing your obvious horror, he stalks off in a huff. Demeter explains: “A nymph loved Hermaphroditus and wanted to remain joined to him forever. Zeus granted her wish, and the two merged into a single being. Be careful what you wish for.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.0.39.0.messa: You see a white poplar. “That used to be Leuce, whom Hades loved. I no longer remember why, but he changed her into a white poplar to protect her. Strange man.” She shakes her head and waits for you to finish examining the chest.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.104.40.0.mes: You meet an old blind seer. He introduces himself as Tiresias. He explains that Hera blinded him because he took Zeus's side. Zeus, however, rewarded him with the gift of prophecy. “Come inside, and I shall show you everything you need to know.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.105.31.1.mes: A place of wonder and beauty stretches before you. These must be the Elysian Fields. You hear the laughter and happy voices of their inhabitants. Children and adults play and laugh here, and will do so for all eternity.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.112.32.1.mes: As always, your mother creeps up unnoticed and starts lecturing you about washing behind your ears and eating properly. You listen for about an hour before your father rescues you. Fortunately, they leave before she turns to more personal matters. Your men snicker behind your back for days afterwards.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.113.136.0.me: You see several men sitting in a flowery meadow, trying to keep a fire going. As you approach, one comes to meet you. “Greetings, I am Acastus, one of the Argonauts. We became separated from the others and are looking for a way off this little island. Please take us with you.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.12.46.0.mess: “Thank you for getting rid of those beasts,” says a graceful woman dressed in earthy colours. “I hate it when those undead try to reach my island. Since you helped me, I shall show you around personally. Come.” She beckons you to follow. And who are you to argue with a goddess?
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.123.128.0.me: As you approach the mill, you see an ugly old crone. You recognise her as the crone of the mill, goddess of the moon and fate. She says: “You know who I am. That is surprising, since half the goddesses are in charge of the moon. At least I'm not just another pretty face.” You nod. She teaches you a new spell.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.123.52.0.mes: As you approach, she turns to you and resurrects those who fell in the sea battle. She adds them to your ranks, bringing life to the dead.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.123.53.0.mes: Directly ahead, you see Alcyone, goddess of the sea, sitting among the sirens. She can bring life to the dead and death to the living. The moment she sees you, she sends her nagas against you to bring death to the living!
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.125.109.0.me: As you leave after dinner, Circe offers you this pendant to ease your travels at sea.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.126.109.0.me: A lovely woman approaches and introduces herself as Circe. She invites you to dinner. You all behave politely and spend a pleasant, peaceful evening with her. At last she declares: “You are much nicer than Odysseus and his swinish companions. I am glad some people have not forgotten their manners.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.128.24.1.mes: As you approach the beach, you see hundreds of translucent souls wading into the waters of Oblivion and drinking deeply. Once they have drunk, they shoot upwards and disappear. Perhaps you should not get too close to the water.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.131.65.0.mes: You encounter an enormous man with a large hammer, working hard on something. You cannot tell what. “Who are you?” he asks gruffly. You introduce yourself. “I am Hephaestus. Go away.” You know of him. He displeased the gods, and Zeus sent him here to Lemnos as punishment.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.134.69.0.mes: You see a forge in the distance. The clang of steel echoes through the valley. Someone is hard at work here. Unfortunately, there are other creatures here too, perhaps guards.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.135.117.0.me: A sudden sharp pain wakes you, and you realise you have been tricked. This is Procrustes, robber and murderer. He ties his victims to a special bed, stretching the short ones and cutting down the tall ones. Suddenly he cries out in surprise. The noise of your soldiers drives him away before he can kill you.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.135.118.0.me: After the battle, you lose your way and meet a kindly old man. He offers you a little supper and a bed for the night. You notice his arms are unusually strong for his age. He takes you to his house, where you enjoy a good meal and settle down to sleep.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.136.58.0.mes: As you approach the whirlpool, you call to Aeolus, who lives on the islands. You tell him the gods want you to descend underground. He obliges, unleashing winds unlike any you have ever known. They create a mighty whirlpool that carries you into the underworld.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.136.95.0.mes: After landing, you see a beautiful sea nymph strolling along the beach. She invites you to join her. A little voice inside whispers: “Isn't that Calypso, who delayed Odysseus on his way home? Don't promise her you'll stay!” You follow your own good advice and decline. The furious nymph curses you.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.137.4.1.mess: ANYONE UNPREPARED PROBABLY WON'T LAST LONG...
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.138.136.0.me: After landing on the island, you meet two people, a father and son. The father tells you where you are: “You are on the tip of Crete. My son Icarus and I are about to fly away on these wings I made.” You notice each carries a pair of wings. Not a bad way to travel. You bid him farewell.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.138.136.1.me: You enter the dark labyrinth and discover that other inhabitants have settled here too. It seems the Minotaur did not suffer from loneliness. You hope this expedition will be worthwhile.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.139.55.0.mes: You meet an old man living in the caves. He introduces himself as Aeolus, keeper of the winds. He releases them at the gods' command. You talk for a while, and he is grateful for your company. “Walk a little way along the beach and you will find something nice. It is yours.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.14.106.0.mes: You reach for the fruit, but your hand passes straight through it. A mere illusion! Someone laughs. “Nice try, mortal, but do you really think we would leave it so easily within reach? Haha!” You blush scarlet. “Ha ha! You are amusing. Such entertainment deserves a gift.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.14.13.0.mess: I GAVE YOU THAT STRENGTH TO TEMPT YOU WITH WHAT IS HERE
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.142.131.0.me: You see a large cave entrance leading deep underground. You realise this is what Daedalus was talking about. This must be the entrance to the Minotaur's lair. Perhaps Pasiphae is still alive and will help you find the Titan's Cuirass.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.15.107.0.mes: You round the mountains and see a beautiful tree nearby. Wondrous fruit hangs from its branches. It must be ambrosia! You want to hurry, but there is one small problem: the way is blocked! Never mind, you can surely deal with these beasts easily enough and continue.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.17.24.1.mess: You stop at a nearby lake for a drink. You notice a man who can neither lower his head far enough to drink from the lake nor reach the fruit hanging just above him. You decide it is best to leave Tantalus to his torments and hurry on.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.19.89.0.mess: Now you remember: it is him. His wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus killed him and Cassandra upon their return. According to the story, his other two children, Orestes and Electra, later killed their mother and her lover when Orestes returned to Mycenae.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.19.90.0.mess: As you approach the tomb, you recall the story of a man named Agamemnon. A hero of the Trojan Wars, he received Priam's daughter Cassandra as his spoils. Wasn't he also the man who sacrificed his son Iphigenia to secure favourable winds for the Greek ships?
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.21.124.0.mes: These are the sirens whom Demeter changed into strange creatures for failing to protect her only daughter, Persephone. Once beautiful nymphs, they are now embittered by what Demeter did to them.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.21.67.0.mess: As you approach the pair, the man calls out: “What do you think? Would that statue deserve the gods' blessing? Please look closely and tell me your opinion.” Even from here, you can see it certainly deserves their blessing. You tell him so, and he beams with pride.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.22.66.0.mess: You see a man and a beautiful woman picnicking near a statue. They are discussing its merits. The woman says: “Aphrodite may not bring it to life as she did me, but I am certain it is very well made. Don't worry so much, my dear Pygmalion.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.23.110.0.mes: Now you know this well-guarded island can hold nothing but ambrosia, the life-giving fruit of the gods. You immediately begin searching in earnest. After all, anyone who eats even a mouthful gains eternal life. What a wonderful thing!
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.24.26.1.mess: You encounter a tormented soul, hardly unusual in these parts. It is Sisyphus, once the wicked king of Corinth. He is now condemned to roll an enormous boulder uphill, only for it to roll back down before he reaches the top. You hurry past before the stone returns and crushes you.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.25.112.0.mes: You have no idea which way to look for ambrosia, if it is here at all. But you see several groups of creatures apparently guarding something very important. Who knows? Perhaps it really is here.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.26.101.0.mes: You meet three graceful, enchanting women. They welcome you warmly and ask you to stay a while. At last you realise they are the Graces. Awestruck by their presence, you try to impress them, but amuse them instead. They give you a gift.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.26.44.0.mess: A young man approaches and challenges you to wrestle. You accept without hesitation and defeat him after a long struggle. He says: “The only other person to beat me was Theseus. You are a great warrior indeed. My name is Cercyon.” He leaves, forgetting his bag. You look inside.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.27.28.0.mess: You see a man playing a lyre, setting the final stones of this hilltop fortress in place. He greets you and says: “I am Amphion the musician. Hermes taught me to play, which is why the stones move to the sound of my lyre.” He shows you a few tunes, and you go to inspect his newly built fortress.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.27.39.0.mess: You notice the River Alpheus flowing through the stables. Then you realise these are the Augean stables, into which Hercules diverted the river to clean them. You are very glad he did, since they stink even with the river. Imagine if it were not there!
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.27.42.0.mess: You see the burial mound of the great Amazon queen Penthesilea. A notice on a tree reads: “Here rests Penthesilea, the brave Amazon who fell during the siege of Troy. May her soul find peace in the Elysian Fields.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.28.26.1.mess: You have reached Tartarus. The journey was long and arduous, but at last you are here. Here the damned souls are held in their eternal hell. Tormented and disfigured, they wail without cease. You know these hideous souls will stop at nothing to devour you.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.29.25.1.mess: Upon entering Tartarus, you are welcomed by Hypnos, son of Night. He gives you and your troops refreshing rest and eases your pain. To make your onward journey easier, he gives you a gift. You thank him and continue.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.3.43.0.messa: You see a beautiful laurel beside the road. Demeter tells you it was once a young woman named Daphne. Apollo pursued her, but she wanted none of his attentions. “She begged me to turn her into a tree, so I chose a laurel. Now she is quite happy in my garden.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.31.27.0.mess: After the battle with the lizardmen, you notice one of them changing into a human. “Thank you for freeing me from that loathsome form. I foolishly mocked Demeter, and she turned me into a lizardman. Take my shield and use it for good.” He dies, and you take his shield.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.32.24.0.mess: You approach the tent and see a group of men leaving. You strike up a conversation with their leader, Achaeus. He tells you he is returning to Thessaly to reclaim the estate his father was deprived of.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.37.23.0.mess: You study your map, wondering where these mountains came from. Your deputy tells you of a couple who dared to take the names Zeus and Hera. What followed was probably the only decision the two gods ever agreed upon. They turned the two mortals into these mountains.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.37.69.0.mess: You see a deep ravine formed after the fall of Troy. You know it swallowed Priam's daughter Laodice during the city's fall. It is always best to keep away from such places.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.4.15.1.messa: You carefully skirt a tormented man lying on the ground. It is Tityos, who assaulted Leto. As punishment, he must lie stretched upon the ground forever while two vultures endlessly peck out his liver.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.4.19.1.messa: You pass a man bound to a spinning wheel of fire. You remember the story of Ixion, king of the Lapiths, a thoroughly wicked and depraved man. The gods punished him with eternal torment in Tartarus. You thought your mother had invented the story to make you behave. Aren't you glad you listened?
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.41.66.0.mess: A flock of seven doves circles the tower. You recall the story of the Pleiades, the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione. Zeus changed them into doves to protect them from Orion's advances.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.42.41.0.mess: As you approach the observatory, you see twins playing in a flowery meadow. They drape you with garlands, and you join their singing and dancing. You learn they are the goddesses Flora and Fauna, protectors of women, youth, flowers and spring. They leave you a small gift.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.44.27.0.mess: This is Dionysus's castle. A river of wine flows from beneath it into the valley. The sounds of merrymaking and laughter carry clearly. The guards are plainly completely drunk, singing out of tune at the tops of their voices. Wine pours over the walls.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.44.41.0.mess: You approach a magical circle where beautiful little winged girls frolic around a woman. Her long hair ripples with every movement, like poetry in motion. She beckons you to join them, and you gladly oblige. After hours of merrymaking, she tells you her name is Ariadne and she is Dionysus's wife.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.44.59.0.mess: This is the Valley of Learning, dedicated to Athena, goddess of wisdom. Every school of thought and training has gathered here to educate all who pass through.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.45.33.0.mess: Three people sit in the garden: two kings and a woman. She is negotiating a peace treaty between the two hotheads. You decide to listen; perhaps you will learn something. You discover the negotiator is Amphictyonis, goddess of friendship between nations!
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.46.15.1.mess: After defeating the crones' wyverns, you quickly kill their mistresses too. As you pass the corpses, one of your men spots an eye. It turns out to be a dragon's rather than a human's. You examine it and put it in your pocket. It might hold some magical power.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.47.36.0.mess: You find an Endless Purse of Gold dropped here by Dionysus. He seems to be growing forgetful in his old age. Or perhaps he left it here in a drunken stupor.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.48.131.1.mes: After landing, you meet a sad young woman. Seeing how lonely she is, you talk with her for a while. She tells you she is Persephone, wife of Hades. She lets you explore her private grove, the only living place in the underworld.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.48.33.0.mess: Rounding the mill, you see a beautiful young girl. She giggles and beckons. Enchanted, you follow her through the river, losing coins and gems without caring. When you fall over, you discover this is no ordinary river, but a river of wine. You and your men drink deeply and joyfully.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.48.36.0.mess: One flower beside the lake stands out: a narcissus. You recall the story of a handsome youth named Narcissus who rejected the nymph Echo's love. She condemned him to love his own reflection in a pool. This must be him. His example encourages you to be humble.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.48.57.0.mess: You see a man weeping. He explains that he is Midas, and everything he touches turns to gold. He has not eaten for ages and has even turned his daughter to gold. He will be freed only if someone kills those beasts. He has this bag to offer as a reward.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.49.126.1.mes: You see a woman sitting idly beside the fountain. She introduces herself as Styx. You recognise her as a nymph, and a very beautiful one. You remember she helped Zeus defeat the Titans. As a reward, she may wander freely wherever she pleases. Since then she has befriended Persephone.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.49.33.0.mess: The next day, you wake in the river of wine with a dreadful hangover. You ask a centaur who the woman was, and he laughs. “That was Ate, goddess of delusion, mischief and guilt.” You feel guilty for wasting a day of your quest, and you are missing soldiers as well!
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.49.42.0.mess: A woman sits quietly in the clearing, a beautiful ring adorning her finger. She looks up and says: “I am Eirene, goddess of peace. I see you have travelled far and have many trials ahead. Take this ring. It will help you negotiate better and avoid battles.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.49.55.0.mess: As you approach the shrine, you realise you are on Mount Helicon. This shrine is dedicated to the Muses. You had better be very courteous and well behaved here. It would be unwise to anger the Muses.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.5.38.0.messa: You almost trip over a handsome sleeping youth. Demeter warns you just in time. She explains: “That is Endymion, whom Selene, goddess of the moon, loved. He was granted eternal sleep so that he might remain young forever.” What a price to pay.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.50.66.0.mess: As you approach the school, a beggar comes up to you. “A coin, sir?” he pleads. “I am Bellerophon, unjustly slandered. I was forced to fight the Chimera. I won only with Pegasus's help. He has retired now, and my travels have cost me all my money.” Taking pity, you toss him a few coins.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.52.26.0.mess: You encounter an old, wrinkled man and recognise the poor fool. It is Tithonus, to whom Zeus granted eternal life at Eos's request. But Eos forgot to ask for eternal youth, so each year he grows older and more decrepit. Naturally, she no longer loves him. The wretch.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.52.39.0.mess: Looking more closely, you see the scholarly-looking man tending several beehives. He beckons and says: “Don't worry, the bees are friendly. Would you like some honey? My name is Aristaeus.” He notices your puzzled expression. “Apollo's son. I invented beekeeping.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.54.122.1.mes: You see a beautiful young woman on a bench among the trees. As you approach, she greets you cheerfully and tells you her name is Persephone, wife of Hades. This is her private grove. You talk with her for a while, easing her loneliness. She lets you explore the grove.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.54.123.1.mes: Your soldiers are heartened by the kindness you showed such a lonely and lovely young woman.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.54.37.0.mess: As you approach the graceful statue, you recall a story your mother once told you. It concerned a nymph named Arethusa, whom Artemis turned into a fountain so she could escape Alpheus. If this is her, she has found the perfect resting place.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.54.63.0.mess: You encounter a man teaching several young people. It is Cadmus, inventor of the alphabet. Apparently he is teaching the youngsters to read and write. Unwilling to miss such an opportunity, you join them. You leave knowing far more.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.54.94.0.mess: You meet a woman holding an ornate box. She tells you her name is Pandora and she was created to unleash every misery upon humanity. “There is no hope,” she murmurs. Unable to contain your curiosity, you force the box open to look inside. Hope flies out. “Thank you!” the woman cries.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.54.95.1.mess: It seems the souls of the dead summoned by Odysseus never bothered returning whence they came. Or perhaps they could not return, and dislike the prospect of spending eternity here.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.54.96.1.mess: Directly ahead is the pit Odysseus dug to summon the spirits of the dead. He poured milk, honey, wine and water over the place and sprinkled it with white barley. Only when he cut the throats of a ram and a ewe did the spirits arrive and answer his questions.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.55.30.0.mess: You meet Alcmene, mother of Hercules, beside the spring. She is extraordinarily beautiful and wise. Thinking you might learn something from her, you sit down and discuss many things. After a while she goes home, but much of what she taught you stays in your memory.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.55.74.0.mess: This is the Valley of Learning, dedicated to Athena, goddess of wisdom. Every school of thought and training has gathered here to educate all who pass through.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.56.32.0.mess: You see a handsome youth resting beside a pool full of gems. He plays a captivating tune on his flute. Soon you forget everything else, throw down your weapons and begin to dance. You dance all night until you fall asleep from exhaustion. The next morning he is gone, along with some of your gems!
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.56.62.0.mess: Here in the clearing, Hermes is teaching his pupils the art of oratory. You try to slip past unnoticed, but he will not let you leave until you have heard the rest of the lesson. So you sit among the others and learn against your will.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.57.101.1.mes: It seems strange that such a place could exist in Hades's underworld. Yet here, in the realm of the dead, a beautiful green strip winds through the emptiness of the underworld.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.58.98.0.mess: You meet two men arguing on the road. They draw swords, and the younger kills the elder. “I am Oedipus. I didn't even know his name, but he was a stubborn fool who drew his sword on me.” You nod; you saw it all.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.59.98.0.mess: A few steps later, you remember what the Delphic oracle said of Oedipus. He was destined to kill his father Laius, so his father left him to die. Apparently he survived. You glance back at the departing youth. Your good deed today will be to spare him the knowledge that he has just killed his father.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.61.7.0.messa: This is the ancient Greek city of Abdera. Hercules founded and named it in memory of his good friend Abderus, who accompanied him on some of his labours. Abderus was eaten alive by Diomedes's mare. Hardly a pleasant end.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.63.46.1.mess: Passing through this sorrowful valley, you remember a lost love. The memory tears at your heart. You continue in grief.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.63.64.0.mess: A group of Silver Pegasi guards this valley. Originally, only centaurs lived here. Over time, however, all manner of wondrous beings settled in the fertile valley.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.65.57.1.mess: You see souls sitting on the jagged hills, unable to enter the valley. Among them is Ajax, hero of the Trojan War. He killed himself in shame after jealousy drove him mad when Agamemnon awarded Achilles's armour to Odysseus. You decide not to linger and continue.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.65.58.1.mess: On your journey, you enter the Asphodel Fields. You know the souls unable to pass through the Vale of Mourning dwell here: those who died in childhood, were condemned to death on false charges, or took their own lives. You pity these poor lost souls and their fate.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.65.62.1.mess: Directly ahead you see Cerberus, the three-headed dog charged with protecting the land of the undead from those who do not belong. That includes you. You notice there are many Cerberuses here! After his embarrassment with Hercules, he seems to have acquired a few extra copies of himself, just to be safe.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.65.63.1.mess: Charon tells you: “You will pay me on the other shore when I ferry you back. Until then, I shall wait here.”
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.65.90.1.mess: Charon the ferryman now demands payment for taking you across Lake Cocytus. He extends a bony hand and accepts the gold coin you offer. He climbs back into his boat and waits patiently.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.66.52.0.mess: The man rescued from the clutches of the hideous cyclops rises and runs to his wife. She cries: “Acis, you're alive! Thank the gods!” He answers: “Yes, Galatea, I am all right. Fortunately, these kind people killed Polyphemus. Now we can live in peace.” They hurry away, but leave you a small gift.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.70.12.1.mess: You see a man bound to a chair. A sign reads: “Here sits Peirithous, so that he may abduct no more women.” You know he helped Theseus abduct the Amazon Antiope, and later Helen. He must have tried to take Persephone too, to have angered Hades so much. Fool.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.70.33.1.mess: At last! You are out of that gloomy valley. Ahead stands a group of men and women chatting casually. Nearby, another group practises fighting. Curious, you approach. What does the sign say about this place?
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.71.80.0.mess: You come upon a footrace. An extraordinarily swift woman overtakes a young man. He falls to his knees and begs for mercy, but receives none. He is killed at once. Another young man challenges her. He is relying on three golden apples, each more tempting than the last, to delay her as she picks them up.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.72.80.0.mess: The young man's trick succeeded, and he won the right to marry Atalanta the huntress. Delighted, he lifts her off the ground, making her sandals fall off. You quietly pick them up and put them on. A fine fit.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.73.117.1.mes: You did not believe the sign, so you decided to discover whether your true dreams hung from this tree as well. After dreaming of immense riches, you realise you should have trusted it. Now your dreams of wealth are gone, along with some of your valuables!
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.73.77.0.mess: Curious, you stop and ask someone who the couple are. He replies: “That is Acontius and Cydippe. Acontius swore by Artemis that he would marry Cydippe. She was to marry another, but became so ill that her father is forcing her to marry Acontius.” You leave a small gift on the table and continue.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.74.32.1.mess: After defeating Achilles and his men, you find the little item he was hiding here. Hector is immensely grateful, thanking you again and again for allowing him to take revenge on Achilles.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.74.77.0.mess: In the clearing ahead, you see a young couple getting married. The groom and his family look extraordinarily happy, but the bride is less enthusiastic. Her parents look very stern, and she looks quite ill. You approach, intending to pass the wedding party.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.77.25.1.mess: You peer into Hades's terrifying underground realm, glad you need not spend much time here. There is unbearable heat, dangerous lava flows and active volcanoes. Not to mention some of his pets.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.8.133.1.mess: BUILD UP YOUR STRENGTH HERE AS THE NECROMANCERS
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.80.141.1.mes: You enter the land of the dead, wondering why Aeneas chose this route. It is barren and inhospitable, full of unimaginable horrors. You begin to wonder why you entered this lifeless void at all. Nothingness surrounds the narrow path. Your soldiers do not like it one bit.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.80.86.0.mess: A group of unicorns guards this valley. Originally, only centaurs lived here. Over time, however, all manner of wondrous beings settled in the fertile valley.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.94.104.1.mes: You see a woman sitting on something meant to be a chair. She leaps up and embraces you. “Thank you for rescuing me! Take everything you can carry. Just get me out of here.” You agree to take Pasiphae somewhere safe. In gratitude, she gives you a helmet.
map.[roe] - maturita.guards.94.143.0.mes: You approach the gate to the underworld, and all those stories begin to frighten you. Gathering your courage, you continue, watching warily for the lost souls and dreadful creatures said to dwell below.
map.[roe] - maturita.header.description:
THIS MAP IS QUITE CHALLENGING – I RECOMMEND PLAYING AS A TEAM.
YOU WILL NOT FIND TOWN PORTAL, FLY OR
DIMENSION DOOR IN ANY TOWN ON THE MAP. YOU HAVE A CHANCE OF ACQUIRING THESE SPELLS (WITH DIFFICULTY)
IN BOOKS. THERE ARE PLENTY OF ARTIFACTS AND TREACHEROUS PLACES.
OBJECTIVE: DESTROY THE OTHER ALLIANCES.
AUTHOR: KOVOS ---GOOD LUCK :-)

map.[roe] - maturita.monster.0.14.1.mess: “So you've come to take my Titan's Cuirass? Good luck, you little weakling! Bwhahahahahahahaha!”
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.107.25.1.me: You encounter men re-enacting the great Trojan War. They seem to think of nothing else down here. Then again, most of them were doing just that when they died.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.110.29.1.me: A group of squabbling men catches your attention. They are deceased zealous monks, gathered here to discuss theology and other lofty ideas. What else would they do for all eternity?
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.113.135.0.m: Grateful that you will take them off this little island, they empty their pockets into your treasury.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.113.21.1.me: This appears to be centaur territory. They frolic in the fields and bathe in the lake. As you pass through the forest, they stop and talk to you.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.121.25.1.me: It seems horses can accompany their masters even after death, provided they fall together in battle. A group of champions is practising with lances. You decide joining them might be fun.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.122.21.1.me: The dwarves of the Elysian Fields frolic here. Men, women and children lounge about, enjoying themselves. Spotting an intruder in their eternal happiness, the men quickly form ranks and decide what to do with you.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.130.22.1.me: A group seems to have gathered for an archery contest. They ask whether you want to join. When you decline, they decide to use you for target practice.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.136.49.0.me: You encounter a medusa, though not the original. Her head is hidden in a bag, after all, but her offspring are no less deadly. These women may not be as beautiful as the original, but what can you expect from cheap imitations?
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.28.30.0.mes: You approach the sea monster Addanc and its companions. They torment travellers trying to sail on Lake Ilyon. You decide it would be best to get rid of the loathsome creatures.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.28.59.0.mes: A motley band of thieves leaps from the bushes, led by a dashing man. He introduces himself as Sceiron and says: “Give me all your gold, and I'll let you go. Otherwise, I'll throw you into the sea for a turtle to eat.” You decline his kind offer.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.28.91.0.mes: You encounter a demon with a single horn, plainly missing the other. He shouts: “I'll get you one day, Hercules!” His friends try in vain to quiet him.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.31.92.0.mes: Surprisingly, the giant looks as though he is already dead. When asked, he explains: “I am Anteaeus, son of Poseidon, invincible as long as I touched the earth. Hercules killed me by lifting me up and strangling me. Since my burial, I have slowly been coming back to life.”
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.34.93.0.mes: You approach two cyclopes whose feet are tied to a club. They struggle desperately to free themselves, but cannot agree how. Tired of their quarrelling, you untie their feet. Awkwardly, they declare: “We won't fight each other any more, but you're another matter!”
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.47.15.1.mes: You encounter three crones who share a single eye and a single tooth. They quarrel and fight constantly. You tell them to step aside and let you pass, but they cackle gleefully. “Send the wyverns at them! We'll cook them into soup!” Wyverns rush out of nowhere and attack savagely.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.49.41.0.mes: You see a drunken young man and his companions harassing several lovely girls. Chivalrously, you intervene, telling them to stop and go sleep it off. Their leader, Comus, decides to start a brawl. You have no intention of backing down, and are glad the god of revelry and feasting is blind drunk.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.57.75.0.mes: The centaurs guard their valley well, admitting only those who come in peace.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.61.18.0.mes: As you approach the archers, one catches your eye. He shoots an arrow with such force that it bursts into flame! What an amazing skill! Then you remember he is Acestes, the Sicilian archer whose skill is unmatched.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.64.19.1.mes: You recognise this creature. It is Typhon, father of violent and destructive winds. It seems Zeus imprisoned him here too. He says: “Once I destroy you, I shall be free. Come, friends! Let us unite and free ourselves. Many more of his kind gather and attack you.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.64.28.1.mes: “Greetings. My name is Sarpedon, another soldier from the Trojan War. Before that I was king of Lycia in Asia Minor. My parents are Zeus and Europa. I...” You stop listening when you realise he is probably another lonely soldier longing for one last glorious battle.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.65.52.0.mes: You see a cyclops standing over a man he is about to crush. A group of cyclopes holds the man's wife and cheers their leader on. You rush forward and attack.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.65.92.1.mes: You are surrounded by the Erinyes, dreaded goddesses who punish the dead for crimes not yet atoned for. Nothing escapes their sharp eyes. They pursue the guilty swiftly and furiously, giving them no respite. You wonder whether they know about that little incident some time ago...
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.66.30.1.mes: As you approach a group of men, you recognise the one in the middle as Jason! The men around him are the Argonauts. Awed by the presence of such great warriors, you hesitate a moment before approaching.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.72.31.1.mes: “Greetings, traveller. My name is Hector. I was a Trojan prince, killed by Achilles in the battle for Troy. My men and I will join you to defeat him and his rabble.”
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.73.32.1.mes: “Greetings!” calls a cheerful man. “Would you like some combat practice with me? With us, I mean. I've made friends down here. We've been practising together for a while, but someone new would be welcome.” You consider it and agree. “Excellent! My name is Achilles. To battle!”
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.95.38.0.mes: This is Typhoeus, along with several companions, imprisoned here by Zeus. They have decided to seize your ship and sail off to wreak havoc. It is up to you to stop them.
map.[roe] - maturita.monster.96.105.1.me: At last! You have found the Minotaur, and several of his friends too. They attack immediately.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.128.23.1.messa: Welcome to the River Lethe. Only those not yet born, or awaiting rebirth, may drink the waters of oblivion.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.13.47.0.messag: Welcome to Demeter's island. Tours available.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.134.70.0.messa: Welcome to the island of Lemnos.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.18.91.0.messag: Here rest Agamemnon and Cassandra. May they find peace.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.30.94.0.messag: The island of those who hate Hercules.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.65.52.1.messag: This is the Vale of Mourning, home to those consumed by unhappy love.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.70.97.1.messag: Unhappy are the souls of the unburied, for Charon will not ferry them across Lake Cocytus to the other shore.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.71.32.1.messag: Here rest those who won fame in war.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.75.24.1.messag: Welcome to the realm of Hades.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.76.119.1.messa: Before you stands a tree from which false dreams hang.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.82.140.1.messa: To reach the realm of Hades, you must pass the eight terrors of the underworld.
map.[roe] - maturita.sign.82.143.0.messa: Chryse, goddess of gold, guards her private mine. Travellers, beware!

map.[roe] - maturita.town.105.45.1.name: Summer Residence
map.[roe] - maturita.town.111.106.0.even: You are Athena, goddess of wisdom. You intend to prove beyond all doubt that you are the wisest of the gods by finding the cuirass first. Besides, there has been little to do lately. Perhaps you will find a few mortals to torment along the way.
Winning Erechtheus's help was easy. After all, you raised him as your own son. Artemis, goddess of the hunt, was also happy to join forces. She enjoys a good chase as much as you do.

Artemis is teaching Cherion everything she knows about hunting. His thirst for knowledge seems boundless. At a loss what else to do with him, you send him to Apollo. He apparently has a gift for healing too. Apollo welcomes his new pupil enthusiastically.

In one village lives a proud young girl with a great talent for weaving and spinning. You visit her discreetly and inspect her work. It is very fine, and impresses you enough to buy something. Of course, you will tell no one. It would not look good.

Arachne seems as skilled at spinning tales as cloth. She tells everyone she is a better weaver than you! Ha! You decide to teach the mortal a lesson and return to her hut, this time with different intentions.

When you reach her hut, she is boasting to several women that she is better than Athena herself. “Very well,” you say, “let us see how good you really are.” The dark-haired woman pales only slightly, quickly sets up two looms, and you begin. In the end, it is clear you are better.

Seeking a fitting punishment, you declare: “Despite all your spinning, I am still the best. You shall remind the world who its true weaver is.” Her body begins shrinking, darkening and growing hair. You turn her into a spider. No one will doubt you again.

Artemis has a truly enormous dog named Laelaps. Since he causes trouble when alone, she asks you to watch him while she goes adventuring on your behalf. Feeling a little guilty, you agree. After all, he is only a dog, isn't he?

After the last three days, you have decided you prefer cats. That dog has torn up four sets of curtains, chewed three of your best slippers, each from a different pair, and sheds hair everywhere. Worse, he got excited and wet the floor just as you were trying to charm a man!

You tried leaving the dog outside at night, but he howls until you let him in. Naturally, you cannot sleep until then, losing precious beauty sleep. When you play chess, his tail thumps against the table. That dog must go! When you tell Artemis all this, she replies: “He's yours.”

Artemis has made it quite clear she does not want him back either. A nice dog, very friendly, but he demolishes everything in under five minutes. A regular bull in a china shop. You grumble to yourself, with no idea what to do with him. But he certainly cannot stay here!

At last! Artemis arrives and says she wants to take Laelaps with her. She is going to a wedding, and the bride, Procris, loves dogs. She will adore Laelaps, and he will make the perfect wedding gift. You quickly hand over the leash and usher them out. Peace at last!
One of your priestesses met Poseidon. You do not mind at all; it could give you an advantage in the contest. But their conversation contains nothing useful. A pity, though hardly important.

The day after the party, you could have sworn you left your pipes on the hall table. Or was it in the conservatory? Oh well, they will turn up sooner or later. You realise you should not drink so much wine at these parties. It always ends badly.

It seems a satyr named Marysas found your pipes. He played his own at the party, but must have picked yours up after the feast. He challenged Apollo to a contest and lost. Apparently Apollo takes challenges worse than you do. You should not leave them lying around.

It seems Apollo is supposed to kill Orion, Poseidon's son. Poseidon asked that he be spared, and Apollo passed the task to Artemis. She intends to place an image of a hunter in the sky, after Orion's favourite pastime. Not a bad solution.

Aphrodite stops by and explains that a beauty contest is being held. Apparently mortals are arguing over who is fairest: Aphrodite, Hera or Athena. You suspect there is more to it, but agree. You do not expect to win, but will not decline a challenge.

You arrive in Troy, where the contest is to take place. Some fellow called Paris is apparently an expert on the subject. You think he has been bribed. At least he pretends to judge, but finally chooses Aphrodite. Hera storms out, indignant and furious. You shrug and go home

Artemis asks why losing did not anger you. You explain: “First, it is a contest in what one is born with, rather than a skill gained through training and hard work. Second, it was decided in advance. Besides, the point was to anger Hera, and that was worth it. Remembering her expression, you laugh.
Artemis comes to ask permission to speak with Zeus. Apparently Niobe mocked her mother Leto for having only two children. You send her off with your blessing.

Niobe's punishment is rather harsh, but fitting for a woman who slanders the gods. All twelve of her children turn into statues in the garden. Zeus devised the punishment, and you consider it quite appropriate.

Artemis has been rather irritable lately. She turned another hunter who caught her bathing into a toad. That was not so bad. He will spend the rest of his life catching flies and avoiding water snakes. Nothing too terrible. But she is always grumpy and grouchy now.

A very kind pregnant woman from the village often visits the forest, humming and singing to her child. This greatly annoys Artemis, since she frightens the deer and other game. Finally, Artemis loses patience and forbids her to enter the forest. The woman agrees.

You storm around the castle, shouting and overturning barrels. How dare they?! Poseidon and that whore Medusa committed such abominations, and in your temple! They perpetrated this insult on your very altar, and they will pay. Yes, they will pay.

The kind woman who sang in the forest gave birth a few days ago. She took her son Aesculapius into the forest to show him its wonders. She talked and sang to him, angering Artemis. In her fury, Artemis struck her with an arrow and turned her into a songbird. “Serves her right,” Artemis muttered.

Then Apollo arrives and gazes helplessly at the songbird. He picks up the boy, and you realise it is his son. You suggest taking him to Cherion, who could raise him and teach him healing and hunting. Apollo thinks this a good idea and does so. You reprimand Artemis for her cruelty.

The perfect punishment occurs to you. You appear before Medusa without warning. You see fear in her face. Reaching out, you disfigure her face and body. Her lower half becomes a snake, and her face grows so hideous that its very sight will turn people to stone! Her beautiful hair becomes writhing, hissing snakes.

Poseidon places Medusa and her sisters on an island. You clap gleefully at their despair. Then the sisters begin mocking Medusa. She turns them to stone. You decide it would be better if they all had to live there, and all were ugly. So it is done, and your amusement begins.

Artemis complains that all this travelling is awful and dusty. You tell her about a beautiful pool with a refreshing waterfall and lovely flowers. She takes your advice and goes to bathe. Unfortunately, one hunter, a follower of hers, enjoys peeping.

You discover that Artemis has turned the hunter Acteon into a stag. Not such a bad punishment for spying on a goddess. But then you hear hunting hounds barking, and a human voice coming from the stag! Poor Acteon is being attacked by his own dogs!

You quickly decide to restore poor Acteon's human form. The dogs are very confused to find their master instead of a stag. He is delighted not to have been torn apart. You tell Artemis to take more care while bathing. Men are simply like that.

On your travels, you meet a young centaur with a natural gift for hunting. Impressed, you send him to Artemis to learn from her. She too is impressed by his talent and accepts him as a pupil. You would teach him yourself, but have no time.

You are Aphrodite, goddess of love and beauty. You are usually bored, and this is certainly an entertaining diversion. Surely there will be a few mortals to toy with along the way, and of course a few men whose company will help pass the time.
Cupid has always had a weakness for such fun, so he was your first choice. Aeneas was a Trojan hero, making him suitable, you think, for battles and all those serious matters.

Fortunately for you, she has grown up. There is an extraordinarily handsome youth named Pitho here. You show him the delights of a love goddess's company. Just as it should be. Except for that fertility! This must stop! At least you have another perfect daughter to go shopping with.

You have been thinking about it since your second child was born. People ought to be able to enjoy themselves without having children every time. It is seriously harming your divine trade. There must be something to prevent it. You spend the rest of the day deep in thought.

It comes to you in a dream. A piece of sheepskin slipped over it will work perfectly! You quickly obtain some skin and shape it for a man. You try several designs before finding the right one. Excited, you rush to show Zeus. You know he will soon have a use for it.

You rush up to Zeus and tell him about your invention. At first he does not quite understand, but after a brief explanation, he loves the sheepskin idea. So much so that he rewards your efforts with some crystals. What a splendid day!

At a feast in your honour, you taste Dionysus's wine. It is very good and quite strong. Together, you find a quiet spot on his estate and toast love, wine and good cheer. The evening eventually continues as befits such a celebration.

This time you decide you should perhaps carry the child to term. Mainly because Dionysus said how well maternity clothes suit you. You agree; as goddess of love and beauty, you always look good. It will simply be uncomfortable for a while.

Hera visits to see how you are doing. She knows you are not very happy about the whole situation, but bear it bravely. You complain of backache, swelling, puffiness and those dreadful stretch marks. It is so tiresome, forever giving birth to perfect children. This must stop!

A few days later, Hera returns with a strange expression. Smiling far too sweetly, she says she knows how to ease your pain. She strokes your belly, and you feel something strange happening. She chuckles as she leaves. Puzzled, you decide it is time to give birth.

That witch! She has ruined your perfect little boy. Now he is hideous and dreadful. He is so deformed and pitiful that you are ashamed even to look at him. As you ponder what to do, Zeus arrives. One look at the child is enough for him to banish it from Olympus to a shepherd's meadow.

Watching your son Priapus from afar, you realise what a handsome man he could have become. He should have been graceful and noble, rather than horribly deformed. Angered by this injustice, you resolve to take revenge. You know the right opportunity will come.

King Minos of Crete catches your eye. He is handsome and supposedly very gifted. Curious, you go to discover just how gifted he is. The rumours prove true, and you reward his various talents with a few shapely distractions in his castle.

Walking through the halls of Troy, you realise an opportunity has arisen. The local king, Paris, is madly in love with Helen. She is very beautiful and quite certainly married. Besides, he is not entirely right in the head. This could work.

You go to visit Hera. She has her hands full keeping an eye on Zeus. He has been unfaithful again. This time they somehow reached an understanding and made up. But for how long? With charm and skilful flattery, you steer the conversation towards beauty.

Quite casually, you say: “Athena is certainly very beautiful, taking after her father Zeus as she does. Many say I am the fairest, simply because I am the goddess of love. That makes sense, of course. Others say you are the fairest, because you are queen.”

“So who really is the fairest?” Hera asks. “Perhaps we should ask a mortal,” she suggests, accepting the challenge. “Do you think so?” you ask innocently. “Yes,” Hera replies. “I'll ask Athena whether such a contest would interest her.” You agree that you will ask Athena tomorrow.

It is not difficult to persuade the goddess of competition to take part. This will be great fun. You suggest Paris: he is a king and a man of refined taste. All three of you agree, and when he returns from his hunting trip, you will put him to the test.

You know exactly where Paris is hunting and pay him a brief visit. You promise him Helen if he declares you the fairest, and he quickly agrees. You clap gleefully and return to the castle before anyone notices your absence.

The three of you meet in Troy. Paris has returned from hunting and is ready to judge the beauty of three goddesses. He examines each carefully. Finally, he stops before Aphrodite and says: “You, my dear, are the fairest of all.” Furious, Hera storms out.

As promised, you give Helen to Paris. Her husband, however, has a different view of the matter. The Trojan War begins over this extraordinarily beautiful woman. If people must fight, they should at least fight for beauty and love.

Humiliating Hera has not quenched your thirst for revenge. You have decided to prepare something even better for her. Besides, it will also avenge Zeus's banishment of your little boy instead of fixing him. It involves that sweet village girl, Io.

You arrange for Cupid to hide in a tree with his arrows. Zeus walks past the lovely woman and gives her only a brief glance. At that very moment, Cupid's arrow strikes, and he falls instantly in love. Naturally, he makes a complete fool of himself trying to impress her.

It seems Minos's wife Pasiphae has begun slandering you for rewarding him. Angrily, you visit her. “For your prudery, I shall grant you a little desire – for bulls. That is what this is all about, after all.” You leave her stunned and depart, pleased with yourself.

It is perfect. Zeus is utterly smitten and has decided he has had enough of Hera and her nagging. He is madly in love with Io and refuses to give her up. He is even considering making her a goddess. You roll gleefully on the floor, laughing until tears stream down your face. How perfect!

Hera learns everything and has had quite enough. With a war cry, she storms onto Olympus, looking decidedly dangerous. Zeus fears his wife will kill Io, so he turns her into a white dove. Hera is so furious that she turns Io into a white cow!
You hear of Leda, a woman who laid two eggs. That Helen is very beautiful, and Zeus is plainly her father. You wonder how Hera is taking it all, but are certain she is not pleased at all.

This is hilarious! Apparently Pasiphae persuaded an adviser to make a disguise that would attract a bull! It worked, and she gave birth to the Minotaur! Minos is absolutely furious and locked them both in the labyrinth. Could it get any funnier?

Bored, you decide to visit Ares. There is always something happening at his place. Besides, he is very handsome and all muscle. When you arrive, you find he is as bored as you. Apparently the peasants grew angry about all those raids. You cheer him up with a little nighttime fun.

Oh no! Now you are pregnant! That night with Ares seems to have had further consequences. Well, this could be an interesting experience. After the first bouts of morning sickness, swelling, irritability and the other discomforts of pregnancy, you decide enough is enough. Time for a cute little bundle of joy.

Ares stops by briefly to see his new daughter. Apparently he is disappointed she is not tough, strapping and goodness knows what else. Fine, at least you will enjoy dressing her in beautiful silk and ribbons. At least he gave you a nice present.

Motherhood was cute – for about 10 seconds. Then she threw up on your favourite dress. Enough. No more maternal worries. Ding! She is grown up. Much better. Now you can go shopping together, all her emotional traumas are behind her, and she can look after herself. Phew!

map.[roe] - maturita.town.68.132.0.event: You are Poseidon, god of the sea. You usually reject fun and frolics, but your brother Zeus is right: things have been terribly dull lately. Besides, this is the perfect opportunity to show him who is the better member of the family.
The choice was easy. Your wife Amphritrite and son Nauplius eagerly joined forces with you in the search for the Titan's Cuirass.

Those tritons were certainly a good idea. They elected a king named Triton, which is hardly imaginative. Since you have only created males so far, you make mermaids: graceful females to ensure the race continues. They have built a magnificent underwater city. You are very pleased with them.

All that hard work has exhausted you, so you visit your former lover Amymone. She is doing well and has had no trouble with satyrs. The everlasting spring you created for her still flows abundantly, and the countryside is full of fresh beauty. “Of course,” you tell her, “it cannot match yours.”

You feel good this morning. You spent a pleasant evening with Amymone yesterday. You reminisced about old times, and you told her how Nauplius is doing. He enjoys destroying cities and similar amusements. Finally, you repeated the night he was conceived – almost. You borrowed a sheepskin.

The king who usually rules your main castle boasted that he could do your job better! What an insult! You are doing perfectly well. This is ridiculous. Angrily, you visit the insolent mortal. Tritons announce your arrival, and it is truly majestic.

The king trembles in fear as you pronounce his punishment in a thunderous voice. “You shall chain your daughter Andromeda to a rock for my sea monster to devour in three days. Otherwise, I shall raze the city.” After a moment's thought, you add: “After I leave.” You leave him to wash his underwear.

You send the sea monster to devour Andromeda, but some hero appears and rescues her! Worse, he arrived on Pegasus, your own offspring! Such impudence. You will certainly ground that disobedient little horse! But you have other concerns, so you leave them alone.

Remembering your promise to ground Pegasus, you summon him. Flying simply is not for you. You give him a thorough scolding, but he only replies: “It sounded fun, Dad. Sorry.” You confine him to his room for a week.

Theseus comes to visit. He is one of those heroes who run around the world helping people. If you recall correctly, he is Zeus's son. Naturally, Hera is not pleased he exists. Curious, you intend to receive him, but your adviser reminds you of an earlier appointment. You will see him tomorrow.

Theseus tells you: “It seems my son committed abominable acts towards his stepmother Phaedra. He made her an indecent proposal.” It does not seem unusual to you, but then, you are a god. “I would like you to destroy him so thoroughly that not even his body remains. I cannot bear to see him again.”

You think it over for a moment and agree. You have not struck anyone down for ages, and such wayward boys always make excellent targets. As Theseus leaves, you look into the pool and find Hippolytus. He is playing with friends. Taking care to hit no one else, you kill him with a mighty blow.
You see an exquisitely beautiful woman walking along the seashore. Her name is Medusa. You talk for a while and fall in love with one another. She suggests meeting here again tomorrow evening.

Speaking with Hades, you learn something interesting. Apparently Phaedra killed herself a few days ago. She was troubled by having Hippolytus killed when he had done nothing wrong. Feeling a little guilty, you decide to resurrect him and tell Theseus the truth.

Your son Orion asks for help. He was promised the lovely Merope if he could ride across Chios. He completed the task, but was not given Merope. You suggest seducing her, and then she will be his. He thanks you and hurries off to find her.

Orion managed to seduce Merope, but things are not going to plan. Instead of yielding to him, she resists. He is very sad and can do nothing but pine. You try to encourage him, but Cupid's arrow has struck him, and nothing will comfort him.

She has asked for Orion to be killed! What an ungrateful... You leave the thought unfinished. Asking around, you discover Apollo is supposed to kill him. You beg him to spare Orion and place his image among the stars instead. He would be happier there. And he regrets the whole affair.

Apollo kept his word and had Artemis strike Orion with an arrow. His image among the stars shows what he is at heart: a hunter. You are content to know that every night you can look up at the stars and see your son. You were right: he is happier there.

You meet Medusa in a darkened temple. You enjoy her company for the rest of the evening. She is truly beautiful, with a magnificent figure and face. She savours every moment together. As you leave, you notice this is Athena's temple. You hope she did not notice.

You hear Medusa scream and go to her at once. But on the shore you find only a hideous creature with snakes for hair. Horrified, you realise your beautiful Medusa has become this thing. She is so ugly that the sight of her turns mortals to stone.

You quickly take Medusa to an island. Realising she would be too lonely there, you bring her sisters as well. Medusa screams: “Change me back! I cannot bear to live like this.” You reply: “You offended a goddess. What did you expect?”

You realise Medusa is expecting a child. You dislike the whole idea and decide you really do not want another child. With your divine power, you turn it into something entirely different. Medusa will be surprised!

Naturally, Medusa was more than surprised when she gave birth to a winged horse. He is a beautiful white stallion, strong and independent. Within hours, he is on his feet and flying all over Greece. Pleased with yourself, you ignore Medusa's insults.

After a long day at sea, you realise everything would be much easier if the ocean were less turbulent. Pondering this minor problem, you decide it would be pleasant to have someone calm the waters for you. You gather the necessary ingredients and prepare for tomorrow's creation.

You rise early today, knowing it is a good day to create a few servants. Gathering your things, you create beings half human and half fish, who will blow horns to calm the waters before you. It will certainly make for a grand entrance. Excellent.

You briefly survey your faithful followers. First is Erebus, god of darkness, always willing to have some fun. Then there is Rhadamanthus, judge of your realm. Since you gave him the position, he is happy to make time in his busy schedule to search on your behalf.

Isn't it obvious that you are Hades? You are god of the underworld and have a considerable advantage over the other gods. You are better than they are. Besides, their endless quarrels keep distracting them. They will probably be arguing while you search for the cuirass.
map.[roe] - maturita.town.95.28.1.name: Hades's Residence
map.[roe] - maturita.town.96.108.0.event: Riding in your chariot, you meet a lovely little woman named Creusa. She wins your heart, at least for the moment, and you offer her the opportunity of a lifetime. She cannot refuse. You enjoy her company, then return to that little contest.

You are Apollo, god of the sun. You drive your chariot across the sky to bring light to the world. But you have done it for so long that the horses know the way and do not really need you. So you have decided to come down from your lofty perch and look around a little.

Artemis arrives with a centaur. He is a kindhearted creature who has been learning to hunt. Now he is interested in healing. You consider it and agree to teach him what you know. Not a bad idea. He has a natural talent and truly wants to learn.

It seems that insolent satyr got hold of Athena's pipes and now thinks he is better than you! Such mortal arrogance. You decide to put a little fear into people and pay him a visit. At first your arrival startles him, but he soon accepts the challenge

Marsyas is not a bad piper, and Athena's instrument helps him greatly, but you are undoubtedly the best of all. You defeat him easily, without much effort. He humbly hands over the pipes and tries to slip away. Unwilling to let him off so easily, you flay him alive.

Playing the pipes has always been your passion. For a long time, no one doubted you were the best, and that little contest with Marsyas confirmed it. No one came close to your mastery. Now, however, people say Pan is better than you.

It annoys you that anyone could equal you, especially Pan. He is so irritating, and insolent too. People really are whispering that he may be better, though neither loudly nor often. You have no wish to argue or compete over it, so you decide to take a walk.

On your walk, you meet a man whistling a tune. One of Pan's. He tells you Pan is far better than Apollo ever was. He enthuses about how wonderful Pan is, and with every second you seethe more fiercely. Finally, you explode and tell him you are Apollo.

Poor Midas trembles before your wrath. In an instant, you realise you cannot do anything too cruel, or you will gain a bad reputation. But you want some outlet for your anger, and find a solution. “Here is a pair of donkey ears, so the whole world can see what an ass you are.”

The whole business with Pan depresses you, and you decide to give up the pipes forever. Perhaps you will take up the triangle or something similar. Terpsichors hears of it and visits you. She is the Muse of dance and is very sad that you will no longer play for her.

Terpsichors tells you: “I suppose I shall have to stop dancing if you will no longer play for me. After all, I need the accompaniment of the finest piper.” You feel a little better and decide she may be right. She coaxes you a little longer, and soon you are making beautiful art together.

Your son Orpheus married a wonderful woman, Eurydice. Unfortunately, a snake bit her while she was gardening. You told him to hire an exterminator, but children never listen. Parents always know best. Deciding this is no time for a lecture, you suggest speaking with Hades.
Your priest Abaris has offered to join the expedition. Your son Ion looks forward to rampaging around Greece and having a splendid time, just like his father. Well, not _exactly_ like his father.

Orpheus made a bargain with Hades. If he led Eurydice out of the underworld, she would be his again. All he had to do was avoid looking back until he reached the sunlight. Just before she stepped into daylight, he looked back, and she was lost forever.

Grieving, Orpheus lashed out at everyone around him. Unfortunately, he did not spare the Thracian maenads, and insulted them. Just as they were about to tear him apart for his behaviour, you strike him down and kill him. Now he is with Eurydice and very happy in his afterlife.
At a celebration, you meet an exquisitely beautiful woman named Coronis. You cuddle together in the woods and celebrate in your own way.

Coronis is expecting to give birth any day now. She used to take long walks in the forest until Artemis scolded her for frightening her prey. You suggest staying near the house with the birth so close. She agrees it is a good idea and remains near home.

Coronis gave birth to a beautiful little boy, Aesculapius. He is healthy and happy. She decided to take him for a walk in the forest. In doing so, she startled a deer Artemis was hunting. Furious, Artemis struck her with an arrow and turned her into a songbird.

At a loss what to do, you gaze helplessly at the cheerfully singing bird that used to be Coronis. Athena arrives, apologises for Artemis and suggests entrusting the boy to Cherion. He is capable and owes you a debt. You agree it is a good idea and do so.

Troubled about your son, you are visited by Thalia, Muse of comedy and burlesque, who has come to cheer you up. This time she has some interesting verses and dance steps, and wants your opinion. The first begins: “There once was a man from Nantucket...”

After several hours of verses, dancing and even a ballad about Big-Bottomed Lil and Yukon Pete, you feel much better again. She has a real gift for such sauciness. You also like the one that begins: “There once was a man from Brighton...”

Polymnia is preparing a speech and wants your advice. She is the Muse of song and oratory. She is very good at the latter. You listen very politely to her argument for respecting nature rather than polluting it. Not a bad speech, and you decide to start recycling after this century.

In mortal guise, you attend dinner with a friend. There you overhear some gossip. Apparently a woman named Niobe boasts of having borne twelve children, most of whom have left home, and all of whom are doing well. Not bad, you think.

Creusa sends word. She wants to talk. Still captivated by her charms, you visit her and chat for a while. After about three hours of her dull conversation, you grow restless and persuade her to turn from words to deeds. She gladly obliges.

The next sentence freezes your blood. She slandered your mother Leto for having only two children! How dare she! Who does that mortal fool think she is? Angrily, you storm out and find your sister Artemis to tell her. You decide to visit Zeus tomorrow.

Both of you arrive angrily before Zeus with your grievance. He agrees something must be done. He promises to devise a truly fitting punishment. He will carry it out himself, mainly because it angered him too.

Zeus tells you he is planning something truly appropriate, but you must wait patiently for the punishment to be carried out. Unwilling to make him abandon his plan, you bite your tongue and pace the hall for several days.

You discover what Zeus plans for Niobe. He has summoned all her children to the garden. As they sit on the bench, he binds them in place and announces that they are being punished for their mother's foul tongue. Their horrified expressions will remain carved in stone forever.

Niobe does not enter the private garden for several days, but when she does, her reaction proves the punishment effective. She sits on the ground where Zeus stood, all her children staring at her, and the horror is more than she can bear. From now on, mortals will think twice before slandering the gods.

A young woman named Merope prays fervently in your temple. She wants revenge on the young hunter Orion, Poseidon's son. Unwilling to attack him rashly, you hear her out. Apparently she was to be his reward for completing a task, which he did.

Merope's father decided to give her to someone else instead of Orion. So Orion seduced her. Now she wants revenge for the wrong she suffered, since none of it was her fault. You agree he wronged her, but great care is needed.

For the third evening running, you have done nothing but talk with Creusa. As a man of action, you are getting bored. You tell her the contest means you cannot see each other for a while. With luck, she will marry some mortal by then and leave you in peace.

You glimpse an exquisitely beautiful girl. Following her all day, you learn her name is Daphne. She is very shy and timid, but you know she will yield in time. You send her lots of flowers and sweets, hoping she will want to visit your castle. No answer yet.

Still no word from Daphne. She avoids you and has her parents say she is not home. At first you took it graciously, but you know she is hiding in her bedroom. You are a god, after all. Next time you will see her, and you announce this aloud.

You go to Daphne's house, and she escapes through the back door. You chase her, and she cries to Demeter: “Save me!” Suddenly, she raises her arms, which turn brown and sprout leaves, while her feet take root. A moment later, she is a laurel! Apparently she REALLY did not want to see you. Your vanity wounded, you return home.

Calliope, Muse of eloquence and heroic poetry, stops by seeking inspiration. You decide to help, recounting several of your recent heroic deeds. You spend a quiet evening by the fire. After a few glasses of wine, you decide to act out a few ballads yourselves...

With all the other gods having little children, you are delighted when Calliope gives birth to your son Orpheus. He is a beautiful little boy with a bright future. A maid giggles: “The son of Apollo, god of the sun, has a bright future.” You let the joke pass, being far too happy.

map.[roe] - mortal kombat.event.0.descri: Legend has it that every thousand years, the finest warriors of all eight races gather in one place to fight to the death in a tournament called 'Mortal Kombat'. Only the one whose race alone survives can win.
map.[roe] - mortal kombat.event.1.descri: To keep the outcome from being decided at the outset, the Holy Grail lies buried somewhere on the map. Finding it could greatly alter the balance of power in the tournament...
map.[roe] - mortal kombat.event.2.descri: The legend also says that whoever loses nine times in a row will forever be enslaved by the race that wins the fateful tournament.
map.[roe] - mortal kombat.event.3.descri: Your race has already lost eight times...
map.[roe] - mortal kombat.event.4.descri: ...and you have been chosen for the decisive ninth tournament!
map.[roe] - mortal kombat.header.descrip: Before you begin, choose the race you wish to represent in the tournament...

The keys to this underground gate were scattered across the land. Guard your key as you would your own eyes, and let no one take it.
map.[roe] - mrcha.event.1.description:

That is why you must never let anyone take your key.
map.[roe] - mrcha.event.2.description: Whoever commands the creature will also receive immense riches.
